chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning

questions.question: What are the three topics listed under 'This chapter covers'?
questions.answer: Framing a machine learning problem; developing a working model; deploying your model in production and maintaining it.
questions.explanation: Printed in the chapter-covers box.

questions.question: What assumption of the earlier chapters does this page say often fails in the real world?
options: That models need GPUs
That a labeled dataset is already available to start from
That validation sets are necessary
That neural networks can overfit
questions.answer: That a labeled dataset is already available to start from
questions.explanation: The first paragraph states it directly. The other options are not assumptions the page questions.

questions.question: For the chat-app project on this page, what would the input and target be if you framed it as a supervised problem?
questions.answer: Input: the text of a post. Target: a label such as spam / offensive / acceptable (binary or multiclass classification).
questions.explanation: An exercise in the kind of framing taught in section 6.1.1 (p.196); not stated on this page.

questions.question: Which example project on this page involves images, and what user feature does it offer?
questions.answer: The personalized photo search engine: typing a query like 'wedding' retrieves the user's wedding pictures without manual tagging.
questions.explanation: First bullet of the project list.

questions.question: Before reading on, can you sketch the steps you would take to go from 'flag offensive posts' to a deployed model?
questions.answer: Something like: define the task and metric, collect and label data, understand it, prepare it, pick an evaluation protocol, beat a baseline, build a model that overfits, regularize and tune, deploy, monitor, maintain.
questions.explanation: Compare your list with the chapter outline in the map above.

questions.question: Which of these is part of the 'Develop a model' phase as described on this page?
options: Monitoring the model's performance in the wild
Selecting a model evaluation protocol and a simple baseline to beat
Understanding the business logic underlying the customer's request
Presenting your work to stakeholders
questions.answer: Selecting a model evaluation protocol and a simple baseline to beat
questions.explanation: That item is in the 'Develop a model' bullet. Monitoring and presenting belong to 'Deploy the model'; business logic belongs to 'Define the task'.

questions.question: Name the four sub-steps of 'Define the task'.
questions.answer: Understand the problem domain and business logic; collect a dataset; understand what the data represents; choose how to measure success.
questions.explanation: From the first workflow bullet; they correspond to sections 6.1.1–6.1.4.

questions.question: Why does the 'Deploy the model' phase end with collecting data for the next model generation, and what does that imply about the workflow's shape?
questions.answer: Because deployed models encounter new and changing real-world data; collecting it lets you build an improved successor. The workflow is therefore a loop, not a one-way pipeline.
questions.explanation: The bullet lists this as the last deployment step; section 6.3.4 (p.212) covers maintaining your model.

questions.question: Which question is NOT among those listed at the start of section 6.1?
options: What value will they derive from the solution?
How will it fit into your customer's business processes?
Which optimizer should you use?
What kind of machine learning task can be mapped to the business problem?
questions.answer: Which optimizer should you use?
questions.explanation: Optimizer choice is a model-development detail; the other three are verbatim context questions of section 6.1.

questions.question: How does 'Develop a model' relate to the summary of chapter 5?
questions.answer: It reuses chapter 5's procedure: pick an evaluation protocol, beat a baseline, train a model that has generalization power and can overfit, then regularize and tune for the best generalization.
questions.explanation: The page says the template consolidates chapters 4 and 5; compare p.194.

questions.question: Pick the credit card fraud project. Which of the section 6.1 questions do you think most changes how you'd build the model, and why?
questions.answer: Example answer: 'How will your model be used?' — if it blocks transactions in real time, false positives annoy customers and latency limits are strict; if it only flags for human review, recall matters more and latency less. This affects the metric, threshold and model size.
questions.explanation: Open-ended; tests understanding of why context questions drive technical choices.

questions.question: Can you recite the three parts of the workflow and two sub-steps of each without looking?
questions.answer: Define the task (e.g. collect a dataset, choose a success metric); Develop a model (e.g. beat a baseline, regularize and tune); Deploy the model (e.g. ship it, monitor it).
questions.explanation: Self-check against the three bullets.

questions.question: How does the book frame the click-through rate prediction project?
options: Binary classification
Scalar regression
Image similarity ranking
Matrix factorization
questions.answer: Scalar regression
questions.explanation: The page says CTR prediction is a scalar regression task. Binary classification is the fraud/spam framing, similarity ranking is the archaeology framing, and matrix factorization is for music recommendation.

questions.question: Why does the anomalous-cookie project need an object detection model as a first stage?
questions.answer: To correctly crop out the individual cookies from the raw conveyor-belt images before classifying each one as good or bad.
questions.explanation: Stated in the cookie sub-bullet; raw images contain many cookies and background.

questions.question: If the chat app is strictly end-to-end encrypted, what does the book say follows for the spam model?
options: It must be a rule-based system
It must live on the end-user's phone and be trained on an external dataset
It must run on a remote server with access to decrypted messages
It cannot be built at all
questions.answer: It must live on the end-user's phone and be trained on an external dataset
questions.explanation: Encryption prevents the operator from reading messages, so inference is on-device and training data must come from elsewhere. A server with decrypted access contradicts E2E encryption; the book doesn't say rules are required or that the project is impossible.

questions.question: Why is data availability 'usually the limiting factor' at the framing stage?
questions.answer: Because you can only learn to predict a target for which you have training examples with annotations; if such data doesn't exist, you must collect and label it, which may be costly or impossible, so what you can predict is constrained by what data you can get.
questions.explanation: The first framing bullet; the movie-review example requires both reviews and sentiment labels.

questions.question: What changes in the spam project's framing if 'offensive content' is made a separate class?
questions.answer: It becomes a three-way classification task instead of binary classification.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the spam sub-bullet; p.199 then plans labels spam, offensive, or acceptable.

questions.question: Give two reasons why understanding the customer's existing solution (nested if rules, or a human removing cookies) is valuable.
questions.answer: It is the baseline your model must beat to add value, and it contains domain knowledge (and possibly historical decisions that can serve as labels); it also shows how the new system must integrate with existing processes.
questions.explanation: The book asks you to understand existing systems and how they work; the baseline and labeling aspects are inferences linking to p.205 and p.199.

questions.question: Which project does the book say is better handled without deep learning?
options: Credit card fraud detection
Photo search engine
Music recommendation engine
Archaeological site discovery
questions.answer: Music recommendation engine
questions.explanation: The book says it is better handled via matrix factorization (collaborative filtering). The other three are given ML task types without such a caveat.

questions.question: Pick a problem from your own work. Can you answer all four framing questions for it?
questions.answer: A complete answer names the inputs and target (and where labels come from), the task type, the current solution, and at least one constraint.
questions.explanation: Applying the checklist yourself is the best test of understanding.

questions.question: What are the two hypotheses the book says you make once you know your inputs, targets and task type?
questions.answer: (1) Your targets can be predicted given your inputs; (2) the available (or soon-collected) data is sufficiently informative to learn the relationship between inputs and targets.
questions.explanation: These are the two bullets at the top of the page; the book stresses they remain hypotheses until you have a working model.

questions.question: Why does the book say predicting stock movements from recent price history is unlikely to succeed?
options: Stock data is too large to fit in memory
Price history doesn't contain much predictive information
Deep learning cannot handle time series
There are not enough labeled examples of stock prices
questions.answer: Price history doesn't contain much predictive information
questions.explanation: The book's reason is that the inputs lack predictive information, a failure of the first hypothesis. Size is not the issue, later chapters do handle time series, and price data is plentiful and self-labeling.

questions.question: The ethics sidebar gives two objections to a face-based trustworthiness rater. How does the first objection relate to the two hypotheses on the same page?
questions.answer: The first objection (validity: no clear reason trustworthiness would show on a face) says hypothesis 1, that targets are predictable from inputs, is implausible. With no real signal, the model would only learn the labelers' biases.
questions.explanation: This connects the ML-validity argument to the ethical one: when the true signal is absent, the only learnable pattern in the labels is the labelers' prejudice.

questions.question: Why can't the chat app's own messages be used to train the spam detector?
questions.answer: User chats are end-to-end encrypted, so their contents can't be used; a separate dataset must be obtained and labeled.
questions.explanation: Stated in the last bullet; p.199 completes it with tens of thousands of social media posts tagged as spam, offensive or acceptable.

questions.question: According to the book, which part of most ML projects is the most arduous, time-consuming and costly?
options: Hyperparameter tuning
Model deployment
Data collection
Choosing a loss function
questions.answer: Data collection
questions.explanation: The opening sentence of 6.1.2 says this directly. The other steps matter, but the book singles out data collection.

questions.question: Why does the book say 'The AI algorithm said this person cannot be trusted' is not more objective than 'John Smith said this person cannot be trusted'?
questions.answer: Because the model is a learned approximation of human labelers like John Smith; it encodes their judgments and biases, just in a black box that looks more legitimate.
questions.explanation: Supervised learning approximates the labeling function. If people provide the labels, the model approximates those people.

questions.question: Pick a project you'd like to build. Write down your inputs, targets and task type, then judge how confident you are in each of the two hypotheses, and whether the project raises any ethical concerns.
questions.answer: Answers vary; a good answer identifies a concrete reason to believe the signal exists and the data captures it, plus any bias or harm risks.
questions.explanation: This applies the page's checklist (framing, hypotheses, ethics) to your own work before you spend effort on data collection.

questions.question: Which two example projects need no new data collection, according to the book?
options: Cookie flagging and satellite imagery
Music recommendation and click-through rate prediction
Spam detection and photo search
Photo search and music recommendation
questions.answer: Music recommendation and click-through rate prediction
questions.explanation: User likes and years of CTR logs already exist. The cookie and satellite projects need new images and labels, spam needs a separate labeled dataset, and photo search needs manual tagging.

questions.question: What three properties of training data does the book say generalization almost entirely depends on?
questions.answer: The number of data points, the reliability of the labels, and the quality of the features.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph recalling chapter 5.

questions.question: Why does the satellite project need images of each site in different weather conditions?
questions.answer: So that the model sees each site under the range of conditions it will meet in production and learns features of the site rather than of the particular weather. This makes the training data more representative.
questions.explanation: The book states the requirement. The reasoning about representativeness is an inference linked to p.200's warning about nonrepresentative data.

questions.question: What does the book say about the effect of deep learning on the importance of data?
options: Deep learning made data less important thanks to better architectures
Deep learning has only increased the importance of data
Deep learning made data and algorithms equally important
Deep learning only matters for unsupervised data
questions.answer: Deep learning has only increased the importance of data
questions.explanation: The book writes: 'remarkably, the rise of deep learning has only increased the importance of data.' The other options contradict this or are unsupported.

questions.question: What are the three annotation options the book asks you to consider?
questions.answer: Annotate the data yourself; use a crowdsourcing platform like Mechanical Turk; use a specialized data-labeling company.
questions.explanation: These are the three bullets under 'Investing in data annotation infrastructure'.

questions.question: Explain the chain the book draws between the annotation process and model quality.
questions.answer: The annotation process determines the quality of the targets, and the quality of the targets determines the quality of the model.
questions.explanation: A model learns to reproduce its targets, so systematic errors or noise in labeling become errors in the model.

questions.question: You have 50 extra hours on a project whose validation accuracy has plateaued. Based on this page, how would you spend them, and what would make you choose otherwise?
questions.answer: By default, collect more or cleaner data. You might choose otherwise if, say, data is impossible to obtain or the first hypothesis (p.198) seems to fail.
questions.explanation: This applies the book's rule of thumb while recognizing that it is a heuristic ('chances are').

questions.question: According to the book, what is the main downside of using a platform like Mechanical Turk for labels?
options: It is very expensive
It does not scale
Annotations may end up being quite noisy
It requires a medical degree
questions.answer: Annotations may end up being quite noisy
questions.explanation: The book says Mechanical Turk is likely inexpensive and scales well, which rules out the first two options, but labels can be noisy. The medical degree refers to the CT-scan example.

questions.question: Give the book's three examples showing increasing labeling expertise.
questions.answer: Cat vs. dog (anyone), dog breed classification (specialized knowledge), CT scans of bone fractures (pretty much requires a medical degree).
questions.explanation: These appear in the first constraint bullet.

questions.question: The dish app had well over 90% test accuracy yet was wrong 8 out of 10 times in production. Why didn't the test set reveal the problem?
questions.answer: The test set came from the same unrepresentative source (polished foodie-network photos) as the training data, so it measured performance on that distribution, not on users' casual smartphone photos.
questions.explanation: Test accuracy only estimates performance on data distributed like the test set. The book states the root cause: the training data wasn't representative of the production data.

questions.question: You want to rate the sentiment of tweets. What does the book recommend?
options: Train on IMDB reviews since they are well labeled
Train on Yelp reviews, which are short like tweets
Collect and annotate actual tweets from a similar set of users as expected in production
Use any sentiment dataset and fine-tune later
questions.answer: Collect and annotate actual tweets from a similar set of users as expected in production
questions.explanation: The book's advice is to collect data from the environment where the model will be used. IMDB and Yelp data are different domains, and the last option ignores the representativeness requirement.

questions.question: What does the book say to do if you cannot train on production data?
questions.answer: Make sure you fully understand how your training and production data differ, and actively correct these differences.
questions.explanation: Stated at the end of the 'If possible, collect data directly…' paragraph.

questions.question: What do you lose if you don't understand how experts arrive at their annotations, and how serious is it according to the book?
questions.answer: You must treat the dataset as a black box and can't perform manual feature engineering. The book says this isn't critical but can be limiting.
questions.explanation: This is the third constraint bullet.

questions.question: For a model you have built or used, list three ways production inputs could differ from its training data (source, conditions, user population), and how you would check for each.
questions.answer: Answers vary; e.g., different camera quality, different user demographics, different time period, each checked by sampling and labeling real production data.
questions.explanation: This applies the page's representativeness principle to your own work.

questions.question: How does the book define concept drift?
questions.answer: Concept drift occurs when the properties of the production data change over time, causing model accuracy to gradually decay.
questions.explanation: This is the definition at the top of the page, which completes the sentence begun on p.200.

questions.question: In which of the book's examples is concept drift described as 'particularly acute'?
options: Music recommendation
IMDB movie reviews
Credit card fraud detection
Satellite archaeology
questions.answer: Credit card fraud detection
questions.explanation: Fraud is an adversarial context where patterns change practically every day. Music and IMDB are drift examples but not described as acute, and satellite imagery is not discussed here.

questions.question: Why would a model trained on the 2011 IMDB dataset do worse on 2020 reviews than on 2012 reviews?
questions.answer: Because vocabulary, expressions and movie genres evolve over time, so 2020 reviews differ more from the 2011 training data than 2012 reviews do.
questions.explanation: This is the book's explanation. The further production data is in time from the training snapshot, the more it has drifted.

questions.question: What exactly made the 1948 Chicago Tribune phone survey an example of sampling bias?
options: The survey asked too few people
Phone users were more likely to be richer, conservative and Dewey voters, so the collection method was linked to the vote
Respondents lied about their vote
The survey was conducted too early
questions.answer: Phone users were more likely to be richer, conservative and Dewey voters, so the collection method was linked to the vote
questions.explanation: Sampling bias is defined as the collection process interacting with the target. Sample size, lying and timing are not what the book identifies.

questions.question: What assumption does the book say you make whenever you use ML trained on past data to predict the future, and why is it risky?
questions.answer: That the future will behave like the past. It is risky because this often isn't the case, and ML can only recognize patterns it has seen.
questions.explanation: This is from the 'Keep in mind…' paragraph and connects to concept drift and to the market-forecasting warning on p.403.

questions.question: According to the book, what does dealing with fast concept drift require?
questions.answer: Constant data collection, annotation, and model retraining.
questions.explanation: Stated at the end of the first paragraph.

questions.question: Think of a dataset you know. How was it collected, and could the collection process be correlated with the target? How fast would you expect its domain to drift?
questions.answer: Answers vary; look for selection mechanisms linked to the label (opt-in, specific channels or devices) and for domains with fast-changing behavior.
questions.explanation: This applies both sampling bias and concept drift as checks on your own data.

questions.question: Define target leaking in the book's words and give its example.
questions.answer: The presence of features in your data that provide information about the targets that may not be available in production. Example: predicting future cancer treatment from medical records that include 'This person has been diagnosed with cancer.'
questions.explanation: This is the last bullet of 6.1.3.

questions.question: For which kind of problem does the book list accuracy and ROC AUC as common metrics?
options: Class-imbalanced classification
Ranking problems
Balanced classification where every class is equally likely
Multilabel classification
questions.answer: Balanced classification where every class is equally likely
questions.explanation: For imbalanced, ranking and multilabel problems the book recommends precision and recall or TP/FP/FN/TN-based metrics instead.

questions.question: A fraud dataset has 1,000 transactions, 10 of them fraudulent. A model flags 20 transactions, 8 of which are fraud. Compute accuracy, precision and recall.
questions.explanation: This is the imbalanced setting the book mentions. A model that never flags anything would score 99% accuracy with 0% recall, which is why precision and recall are preferred here.

questions.question: Why does the book insist the success metric align with higher-level goals like the customer's business success?
questions.answer: Because the metric guides all technical choices in the project. If it is misaligned, you will optimize the wrong thing and may improve the metric without delivering value.
questions.explanation: 'Your metric for success will guide all of the technical choices you will make throughout the project.'

questions.question: Which exploration step does the book recommend for numerical features?
options: Plot them on a map
Plot a histogram of feature values
Look at a few samples and their labels
Print the number of instances per class
questions.answer: Plot a histogram of feature values
questions.explanation: Histograms show range and frequency. Maps are for location data, viewing samples is for images and text, and class counts are for classification targets.

questions.question: Why might a validation set fail to reveal target leaking?
questions.answer: The leaked feature is present in validation data too, so the model's shortcut works there and the scores look excellent. The problem only appears in production, where the feature is unavailable.
questions.explanation: Inference from the book's definition, which centers on availability in production.

questions.question: For a classification dataset you know, run through the book's six checks. Which one would you expect to reveal a problem, and what metric would you choose?
questions.answer: Answers vary.
questions.explanation: Applying the checklist and the metric guidance from this page.

questions.question: According to the authors, what are the hardest things in machine learning?
options: Choosing an architecture and tuning hyperparameters
Framing problems and collecting, annotating, and cleaning data
Deploying and monitoring models
Writing training loops
questions.answer: Framing problems and collecting, annotating, and cleaning data
questions.explanation: Stated in the 6.2 introduction. Model development (architecture, tuning) is described as not the most difficult step, and deployment is not singled out here.

questions.question: What is data vectorization, and how was it done in the chapter 4 text examples?
questions.answer: Turning any data into tensors (typically floating-point). In chapter 4, lists of integers standing for words were multi-hot encoded into float32 tensors.
questions.explanation: This is the Vectorization paragraph.

questions.question: A feature takes values [100, 150, 200] in the training set. Standardize them to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 (population std).
questions.answer: μ = 150, σ ≈ 40.82, so the normalized values are ≈ [-1.22, 0, 1.22].
questions.explanation: This applies the house-price normalization described on the page: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation, per feature.

questions.question: Why is it unsafe to feed a network data where one feature is in 0-1 and another in 100-200?
questions.answer: Heterogeneous scales can trigger large gradient updates. The gradient for a weight scales with its input value, so the large-range feature dominates and the network may fail to converge.
questions.explanation: The book states the consequence (large gradient updates preventing convergence). The proportionality of gradients to inputs is added explanation.

questions.question: How were MNIST images normalized before training?
options: Standardized per pixel to mean 0, std 1
Cast to float32 and divided by 255
Multi-hot encoded
Left as integers 0–255
questions.answer: Cast to float32 and divided by 255
questions.explanation: This gives values in 0-1. Per-feature standardization was used for house prices, multi-hot encoding for text, and leaving raw integers is what the page warns against.

questions.question: Name the three general preprocessing steps the book lists for 6.2.1.
questions.answer: Vectorization, normalization, and handling missing values.
questions.explanation: Stated in the opening paragraph of 6.2.1. Missing values are covered on p.204.

questions.question: Take a tabular dataset you know (or the house-price data). For each feature, decide whether to divide by a known maximum, standardize, or leave it alone, and explain why.
questions.answer: Answers vary; fixed-range features can be divided by their max, while data-dependent ranges should be standardized with training statistics.
questions.explanation: This practises the two normalization recipes on the page.

questions.question: According to the page, what should you do if a numerical feature has missing values?
options: Fill the gaps with 0
Replace them with the feature's average or median, or predict them with a model
Add a new category meaning "missing"
Always drop the feature
questions.answer: Replace them with the feature's average or median, or predict them with a model
questions.explanation: The book recommends mean or median imputation or a predictive model for numerical features. Filling with 0 is explicitly discouraged because it can create a discontinuity in the latent space. The new-category trick is for categorical features. Dropping the feature is possible but "you don't necessarily have to".

questions.question: In `x -= x.mean(axis=0)`, what is the shape of `x.mean(axis=0)` if x has shape (404, 13), and how is the subtraction carried out?
questions.answer: (13,): one mean per feature; it is broadcast across all 404 rows and subtracted from each.
questions.explanation: Reducing over axis 0 (samples) leaves the features axis. Broadcasting repeats the (13,) vector along the samples axis so each column has its own mean subtracted.

questions.question: Standardize the feature column [2, 4, 6] using the page's two NumPy lines (population std).
questions.explanation: Subtracting the mean gives [−2, 0, 2]; dividing by the population standard deviation (NumPy's default, ddof=0) gives values with mean 0 and std 1.

questions.question: Why does a network trained on data with no missing values fail to handle missing categorical features at test time, and what remedy does the book propose?
questions.answer: It never saw the 'missing' case during training, so it never learned how to respond to it. The remedy is to copy some training samples several times and drop the categorical features likely to be missing, creating training examples with missing entries.
questions.explanation: Models learn only behaviors present in their training distribution. Synthesizing missingness makes the training distribution match the expected test distribution.

questions.question: Why was the stricter mean-0/std-1 normalization not needed in the digit-classification example?
questions.answer: All pixel features share one natural scale (0–255), so dividing by 255 already made the values small (0–1) and homogeneous, which are the two essential properties.
questions.explanation: The page lists small and homogeneous values as the requirements and calls per-feature standardization helpful but optional, citing the digit example as a case that did without it.

questions.question: What guides every modeling decision during model development, according to the start of section 6.2.2?
options: Training loss
Validation metrics that seek to measure generalization
Test-set accuracy checked after each change
The number of model parameters
questions.answer: Validation metrics that seek to measure generalization
questions.explanation: The page says every modeling decision will be guided by validation metrics. Training loss measures fit, not generalization. The test set must not be used for decisions (p.207). Parameter count is not a success metric.

questions.question: Take a tabular dataset you know. Which features would need standardization, which could be missing, and how would you encode the missingness for each?
questions.answer: Open-ended; a good answer distinguishes mixed-unit numerical features (standardize, impute median), categorical features (add a 'missing' category), and identifies features likely to be missing in production.
questions.explanation: Applying the page's rules to a concrete dataset checks that you can tell categorical and numerical handling apart and remember the train/test consistency requirement.

questions.question: Which protocol does the page recommend when you have too few samples for hold-out validation to be reliable?
options: Hold-out validation with a larger validation fraction
K-fold cross-validation
Evaluating on the test set
Training-set accuracy
questions.answer: K-fold cross-validation
questions.explanation: The page states K-fold is the right choice in that case. Enlarging the hold-out fraction shrinks training data and still yields one noisy split. The test set must stay untouched for final evaluation. Training accuracy does not measure generalization.

questions.question: What two requirements must a loss function satisfy, according to the sidebar?
questions.answer: It must be computable given only a mini-batch of data (ideally a single data point), and it must be differentiable so backpropagation can be used.
questions.explanation: Both conditions come straight from the sidebar; they are why ROC AUC cannot be used directly as a loss.

questions.question: Why is crossentropy described as a proxy metric for ROC AUC, and what is the caveat?
questions.answer: ROC AUC cannot be optimized directly, so you minimize crossentropy, which is differentiable and per-sample, hoping that lower crossentropy goes with higher ROC AUC. The caveat is that this is a hope, not a guarantee.
questions.explanation: The book writes 'In general, you can hope that the lower the crossentropy gets, the higher the ROC AUC will be.' The relation is a correlation, so the metric must still be monitored.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three focus areas the page lists for beating a baseline?
options: Feature engineering
Selecting the correct architecture priors
Selecting a good enough training configuration
Adding dropout and L2 regularization
questions.answer: Adding dropout and L2 regularization
questions.explanation: Regularization belongs to the later phase (6.2.5, p.207), after you can overfit. The other three are exactly the bullets on this page.

questions.question: Give an example of how redundant samples between training and validation sets would mislead you.
questions.answer: If duplicate photos (or the same customer's records) appear on both sides, the model can score highly on validation by memorization, overstating how well it will do on genuinely new production data.
questions.explanation: The page warns against redundancy because it inflates validation metrics, defeating the protocol's goal of an accurate estimate.

questions.question: What does 'statistical power' mean in the context of 6.2.3?
questions.answer: Having a small model that is capable of beating a simple baseline.
questions.explanation: The page defines it this way, referring back to chapter 5's common-sense baselines (p.176).

questions.question: For a project you know, write down the success metric, a loss you could train on instead, and a simple baseline you would need to beat.
questions.answer: Open-ended; e.g. metric ROC AUC, loss binary crossentropy, baseline 'predict the positive-class rate for everyone' (AUC 0.5).
questions.explanation: Separating metric, loss and baseline is the practical skill this page builds.

questions.question: Per Table 6.1, what last-layer activation and loss should a multiclass, multi-label classifier use?
options: Softmax and categorical crossentropy
Sigmoid and binary crossentropy
None and mean squared error
Softmax and binary crossentropy
questions.answer: Sigmoid and binary crossentropy
questions.explanation: Multi-label means each label is an independent yes/no decision, so per-unit sigmoids with binary crossentropy fit. Softmax plus categorical crossentropy is for mutually exclusive classes. No activation plus MSE is for regression. Softmax plus binary crossentropy is a mismatched pairing.

questions.question: Which loss and which metric does Table 6.1 list for regression?
questions.answer: Loss: mean squared error. Metric: mean absolute error.
questions.explanation: Regression uses no last-layer activation, MSE as the loss, and MAE as the metric, as in the house-price example (p.153).

questions.question: What are the two hypotheses you implicitly make in a supervised learning project, and what does repeated failure to beat a baseline suggest?
questions.answer: (1) Outputs can be predicted given inputs; (2) the available data is informative enough to learn the input-output relationship. Repeated failure with reasonable architectures suggests one of them may be false, and you should go back to the drawing board.
questions.explanation: The page states both hypotheses and says the answer may not be present in the input data.

questions.question: Why does the book say 'to figure out where this border lies, first you must cross it'?
questions.answer: You cannot know in advance how much capacity the problem needs. Only by increasing capacity until validation performance degrades (overfitting) can you see where the optimum between underfitting and overfitting lies.
questions.explanation: The ideal model stands at the border between undercapacity and overcapacity; the turning point of the validation curve is the only empirical marker of that border.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the three ways the page lists to develop a model that overfits?
options: Add layers
Make the layers bigger
Train for more epochs
Add dropout
questions.answer: Add dropout
questions.explanation: Dropout is a regularizer that reduces overfitting; it appears in 6.2.5 (p.207). The other three increase capacity or training time and are the page's bullets.

questions.question: What example does the page use to show that statistical power is not the same as being powerful enough?
questions.answer: A logistic regression model has statistical power on MNIST but would not be sufficient to solve the problem well.
questions.explanation: It beats a trivial baseline, but its capacity is too low to reach strong accuracy.

questions.question: Without looking, fill in Table 6.1's four rows (task, activation, loss, metrics). Then check yourself against the page.
questions.answer: Binary: sigmoid / binary crossentropy / binary accuracy, ROC AUC. Multiclass single-label: softmax / categorical crossentropy / categorical accuracy, top-k categorical accuracy, ROC AUC. Multi-label: sigmoid / binary crossentropy / binary accuracy, ROC AUC. Regression: none / MSE / MAE.
questions.explanation: Recalling this table from memory is a practical skill you will use whenever you configure a new model.

questions.question: During regularization and tuning, which data should you evaluate each modified model on?
options: The training data
The validation data
The test data
Both validation and test data, averaged
questions.answer: The validation data
questions.explanation: The page explicitly says to evaluate on validation data, not test data, at this point. Training data measures fit, not generalization. Using test data, alone or averaged in, leaks it into model selection.

questions.question: How can a model overfit to the validation process if it is never trained on validation data?
questions.answer: You use validation scores to choose configurations. Over many iterations, the choices adapt to the particular validation samples (including their noise), so the chosen model looks better on validation than it really is.
questions.explanation: The leak happens through human or automated decisions, not through gradients. A few iterations are innocuous; systematic tuning is not.

questions.question: What data should the final production model be trained on, according to the page?
questions.answer: All the available data: training and validation.
questions.explanation: Once the configuration is chosen, validation data is no longer needed for decisions and becomes extra training data; the test set stays separate for the final evaluation.

questions.question: Test performance is significantly worse than validation performance. Which response does the page suggest?
options: Tune further using the test set
Switch to a more reliable evaluation protocol such as iterated K-fold validation
Add more layers
Report the validation score instead
questions.answer: Switch to a more reliable evaluation protocol such as iterated K-fold validation
questions.explanation: The gap suggests unreliable validation or overfitting to it; a more reliable protocol addresses that. Tuning on test data would destroy its value. Adding layers does not fix evaluation. Reporting the inflated validation score is misleading.

questions.question: Why does the page qualify the L1/L2 advice with 'if your model is small'?
questions.answer: Weight penalties are mainly effective for small models; larger models are typically regularized with other techniques such as dropout.
questions.explanation: The page only gives the qualifier. The explanation that weight regularization matters less for large deep networks comes from the chapter-5 discussion of when to prefer dropout (p.190).

questions.question: You validate 100 configurations of equal true accuracy 0.75 on 500 samples. Estimate the standard error of one validation accuracy, and roughly how far above 0.75 the best score might be (use σ·sqrt(2 ln n)).
questions.explanation: This quantifies the page's warning: selecting the maximum over many noisy scores inflates the estimate by several points, which a test set would reveal. (The formula is an approximation added beyond the book.)

questions.question: List, from memory, the five things the page suggests trying in the tuning phase, and say which one you would try first on your own project and why.
questions.answer: Architectures (add/remove layers), dropout, L1/L2 for small models, hyperparameters (units, learning rate), data curation/feature engineering. The order depends on your project.
questions.explanation: Recalling the menu and reasoning about priority checks that you understand what each intervention does.

questions.question: Why do the authors advise against saying 'The model has 98% accuracy' to stakeholders?
options: Accuracy cannot be computed for fraud detection
Most people mentally round it up to 100%
Accuracy is always lower than ROC AUC
Stakeholders prefer ROC AUC
questions.answer: Most people mentally round it up to 100%
questions.explanation: That is the reason printed on the page. Accuracy can be computed for any classifier; it is not always lower than AUC; and the book recommends error rates and counts, not AUC, for stakeholders.

questions.question: In the fraud example, 266 frauds are caught and 14 missed per day. Verify the stated false-negative rate, and compute how many valid transactions per day are implied by 200 false alarms at a 2.5% false-positive rate.
questions.answer: FNR = 14/280 = 5%. Valid transactions ≈ 200/0.025 = 8,000 per day.
questions.explanation: FNR is out of all actual frauds (TP + FN); FPR is out of all actual valid transactions (FP + TN). The 8,000 is implied, not stated.

questions.question: What happens to false-negative and false-positive rates when you lower the flagging threshold, and why must stakeholders be involved in choosing it?
questions.answer: More transactions get flagged: FNR goes down (fewer frauds missed) and FPR goes up (more valid transactions flagged). The right balance depends on business costs (losses from fraud vs. review costs and customer friction), which require business context.
questions.explanation: The page says different thresholds produce different FNR/FPR and that the trade-off requires a deep understanding of the business context.

questions.question: What does the book suggest showing stakeholders who expect the model to 'understand' its task?
questions.answer: Examples of the model's failure modes, such as misclassified samples, especially those where the misclassification seems surprising.
questions.explanation: Surprising errors make it concrete that the model lacks human-like common sense.

questions.question: Which is a reason given on the page for exporting a model to something other than Python?
options: Python cannot run neural networks
The production environment may be a mobile app or embedded system without Python
Exported models are always more accurate
Keras models cannot be saved in Python
questions.answer: The production environment may be a mobile app or embedded system without Python
questions.explanation: The page lists environments without Python and non-Python apps where Python serving adds overhead. Python runs networks fine during training; export does not change accuracy; Keras models can be saved in Python.

questions.question: Why does using a model only for inference open room for optimizations?
questions.answer: Inference needs only the forward pass. Gradients, optimizer state and training-only behavior are no longer needed, so the model can be simplified and transformed to run faster and use less memory.
questions.explanation: The page states that since the production model only outputs predictions, there is room for optimizations that make it faster and reduce its memory footprint; the specific mechanisms are an added explanation.

questions.question: Write a one-paragraph, fraud-example-style statement of performance for a model you have built, using error rates and daily (or per-batch) counts instead of accuracy.
questions.answer: Open-ended; it should name each error type, its rate, the expected counts per time period and their business consequences.
questions.explanation: Practicing this translation is the main skill of 6.3.1.

questions.question: What do TensorFlow Serving and ONNX have in common, according to the page?
options: Both require the model to be written in TensorFlow
Both lift the model weights and a computation graph outside the Python program
Both run only in the browser
Both retrain the model on the server
questions.answer: Both lift the model weights and a computation graph outside the Python program
questions.explanation: That is how the page describes both. Any Keras model can be exported; neither is browser-only; and both serve inference artifacts, not training.

questions.question: Write the line that exports a Keras model for ONNX, and the line that creates the ONNX Runtime session.
questions.answer: model.export("path/to/location", format="onnx") and ort_session = onnxruntime.InferenceSession("path/to/location")
questions.explanation: These are the first two statements of the ONNX snippet; predictions come from ort_session.run(None, input_data).

questions.question: Why does the page compare TensorFlow Serving to the compilation mechanism of chapter 3?
questions.answer: Because TensorFlow Serving serves tf.function computation graphs with a saved set of weights. Exporting traces the model into a static graph, as tf.function does, that can run without the original Python code.
questions.explanation: The page says 'If this sounds a lot like the compilation mechanism discussed in chapter 3 you are spot-on.'

questions.question: Which application is the worst fit for REST API deployment, based on the page's conditions?
options: A web search engine ranking images
A fraud-scoring backend service
A mobile app that must work in airplane mode
A music recommender on a website
questions.answer: A mobile app that must work in airplane mode
questions.explanation: The first condition is reliable internet access, and the page uses exactly the airplane-mode example. The other three are online, latency-tolerant services (p.210 lists several of them as good fits).

questions.question: What typical round-trip latency does the page give for REST serving, and what does that imply?
questions.answer: Around 500 ms; the setup is only suitable when the application does not have strict latency requirements.
questions.explanation: Request, inference and answer together typically take about half a second.

questions.question: If the request is SSL-encrypted, why does the page still say REST is unsuitable for highly sensitive data?
questions.answer: SSL protects data only in transit. On the server the data must be decrypted so the model can see it, exposing it to the server operator or attackers.
questions.explanation: The page states the data must be available on the server in decrypted form.

questions.question: For a model you have trained, decide whether you would export to SavedModel or ONNX and whether REST deployment fits. Justify with the page's three conditions.
questions.answer: Open-ended; a good answer checks connectivity, latency and data sensitivity and names a runtime suited to the target environment.
questions.explanation: Applying the checklist to a real case consolidates the decision criteria.

questions.question: Which project from chapter 6 must run on the end user's smartphone, and why?
options: The music recommender, because recommendations must be instant
The spam detector, because messages are end-to-end encrypted
The satellite imagery project, because images are large
The fraud detector, because transactions are sensitive
questions.answer: The spam detector, because messages are end-to-end encrypted
questions.explanation: The page states that the spam model must run on the phone because end-to-end encrypted messages cannot be read by a remote model. The book lists the recommender, satellite and fraud projects as good REST API fits.

questions.question: Name three practical details that a managed service such as Cloud AI Platform takes care of.
questions.answer: Batching predictions, load balancing, and scaling.
questions.explanation: These are listed explicitly in the paragraph on self-hosting vs. managed services.

questions.question: Why does the bad-cookie detector run 'on device', and how does its situation differ from the usual image of on-device ML?
questions.answer: It has strict latency constraints, so it must run at the factory. Unlike phones or microcontrollers, there are no power or space constraints there, so it can run on a GPU.
questions.explanation: The book shows that device deployment is about location and latency, not necessarily weak hardware.

questions.question: Which statement about TensorFlow Lite is correct according to the page?
options: It requires a different model format from TensorFlow Serving
It runs only on Android
It uses the same TensorFlow save model format as TensorFlow Serving
It is used to train models on microcontrollers
questions.answer: It uses the same TensorFlow save model format as TensorFlow Serving
questions.explanation: The page says this explicitly. TF Lite also runs on iOS, ARM CPUs, Raspberry Pi and certain microcontrollers, and it is an inference framework, not a training framework.

questions.question: Explain the efficiency/accuracy tradeoff mentioned for on-device deployment and what it implies for stakeholder communication.
questions.answer: Memory and power limits force smaller models, which are usually less accurate than the best model on a large GPU. Stakeholders should therefore expect the deployed model to fall somewhat short of the best results seen in development.
questions.explanation: This combines the third bullet with section 6.3.1 on setting expectations (p.208).

questions.question: Give the four conditions under which the book recommends deploying on a device.
questions.answer: (1) Strict latency constraints or a low-connectivity environment; (2) the model can be made small enough for the device's memory/power; (3) highest accuracy is not mission critical; (4) the input data is strictly sensitive and shouldn't be decryptable on a remote server.
questions.explanation: These are the four bullets on the page.

questions.question: For an AR glasses app that labels objects in real time, could you use a REST API? Justify using the page's criteria.
questions.answer: No. The book notes that querying a remote server is not viable for immersive AR because of latency (a REST round trip takes about 500 ms, p.209). The model must run on the device.
questions.explanation: This applies the first bullet, which uses AR as its example.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed on the page as a reason to run a model in the browser?
options: Reducing server costs by offloading compute
Keeping input data on the user's device
Getting higher accuracy than a server model
Working without connectivity after the model is cached
questions.answer: Getting higher accuracy than a server model
questions.explanation: The page lists cost, data locality, latency and offline use. Accuracy is not a reason: local models are typically smaller and slower than server models.

questions.question: What was the original working name of TensorFlow.js, and what does it suggest about its API?
questions.answer: WebKeras. It implements almost all of the Keras API.
questions.explanation: Stated in the JavaScript-deployment paragraph.

questions.question: Why should you avoid deploying a model trained on sensitive data in the browser even if user inputs never leave the device?
questions.answer: The whole model is downloaded to the user's device and so becomes public, and from a trained model it is usually possible to recover some information about its training data.
questions.explanation: The caveat paragraph makes both points.

questions.question: A browser model takes 40 ms on a laptop; the server model takes 10 ms on a GPU. Using the book's network figure, which is faster end to end?
questions.answer: The browser model: 40 ms vs. about 100 + 10 = 110 ms for the server path.
questions.explanation: The book cites an extra ~100 ms network round trip for remote inference. The compute times are illustrative.

questions.question: According to the book, when should you optimize a model for inference?
options: After importing it into TensorFlow.js
Before importing it into TensorFlow.js or exporting it to TensorFlow Lite
Only when deploying via REST
During the first epoch of training
questions.answer: Before importing it into TensorFlow.js or exporting it to TensorFlow Lite
questions.explanation: The book says: 'You should always seek to optimize your model before importing it into TensorFlow.js or exporting it to TensorFlow Lite.' Optimization is not REST-specific, and it applies to a trained model, not to the first epoch.

questions.question: What is the key observation that makes weight pruning possible?
questions.answer: Not every coefficient in a weight tensor contributes equally to the predictions, so the less significant ones can be removed.
questions.explanation: This is the opening of the pruning bullet.

questions.question: Can you explain why the chat app from the spam project ends up using both TensorFlow Lite and TensorFlow.js?
questions.answer: End-to-end encryption forces local inference on every client. Native phone apps use TensorFlow Lite (p.210), while the JavaScript web and desktop versions use TensorFlow.js or ONNX JS (p.211).
questions.explanation: This connects pp. 210 and 211.

questions.question: A model has 60 million float32 weights. Roughly how much weight storage does it need before and after model.quantize("int8")?
questions.answer: About 240 MB before (60M × 4 bytes) and 60 MB after (60M × 1 byte), a 4× reduction.
questions.explanation: float32 uses 4 bytes per weight; int8 uses 1 byte, matching the book's 'four times smaller'.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the control subset in a randomized A/B test of a new recommender?
options: To provide extra training data for the new model
To keep the old process so that outcome differences can be attributed to the new model
To test the model's latency under load
To collect user surveys
questions.answer: To keep the old process so that outcome differences can be attributed to the new model
questions.explanation: The book says the control subset sticks to the old process, and with enough cases the outcome difference is likely attributable to the model. The other options describe unrelated activities.

questions.question: How does the book suggest auditing model predictions in production, and for which two projects does it say you should definitely do so?
questions.answer: Reuse the annotation infrastructure: send a fraction of production data for manual annotation and compare it with the model's predictions. Definitely do it for the image search engine and the bad-cookie-flagging system.
questions.explanation: Stated in the second monitoring bullet.

questions.question: Why does the book suggest user surveys rather than manual audits for the spam and offensive-content flagging system?
questions.answer: The chat app's messages are end-to-end encrypted, so the team cannot sample and annotate production messages, and a manual audit is impossible. User surveys are an alternative signal.
questions.explanation: This combines the third bullet with the encryption constraint from p.210.

questions.question: According to the book, which model has the shortest expected lifespan?
options: Image search engine
Music recommender
Credit card fraud detection
Bad-cookie detector
questions.answer: Credit card fraud detection
questions.explanation: The book gives days for fraud detection, weeks for music recommendation and a couple of years at best for image search. No lifespan is given for the cookie detector.

questions.question: Why can a model be trained in float32 but deployed in int8?
questions.answer: Training needs high precision to accumulate tiny gradient updates, while inference only needs the forward pass to be approximately right. Rounding weights to 256 levels changes outputs very little, so accuracy stays near the original.
questions.explanation: The page notes that int8 models are inference-only and near the original's accuracy. Chapter 18 (p.582, p.585) explains the precision reasoning.

questions.question: List the four things the book says to keep monitoring after deployment.
questions.answer: The model's behavior, its performance on new data, its interaction with the rest of the application, and its eventual impact on business metrics.
questions.explanation: From the paragraph opening 'Even this is not the end.'

questions.question: According to the book, which samples are most likely to help improve the next model generation?
options: Randomly sampled production data
Samples that seem difficult to classify for the current model
Samples the model classifies with very high confidence
Synthetic samples generated from the training set
questions.answer: Samples that seem difficult to classify for the current model
questions.explanation: The book says to pay special attention to hard samples because they are most likely to improve performance. Confidently classified samples add little new information, and random or synthetic samples are not what the page recommends.

questions.question: List the five steps of the 'develop a model' phase in order.
questions.answer: Prepare the data; pick an evaluation protocol; beat a simple baseline (achieve statistical power); scale up to a model that can overfit; regularize and tune hyperparameters on validation performance.
questions.explanation: Straight from the summary's second bullet.

questions.question: Why does the workflow ask you to build a model that overfits before regularizing?
questions.answer: Overfitting shows that the model has enough capacity to learn the training data. Only then is it meaningful to trade capacity for generalization through regularization and tuning; regularizing a model that underfits would make it worse.
questions.explanation: This is the ordering in the summary and section 6.2.4 (p.206).

questions.question: What two questions does the book suggest asking about production data when preparing the next generation?
questions.answer: Are new features becoming available? Should you expand or otherwise edit the label set?
questions.explanation: From the first maintenance bullet.

questions.question: Which is the FIRST step of the deployment phase in the summary?
options: Optimize the model for inference
Monitor performance in production
Set appropriate expectations with stakeholders
Collect data for the next generation
questions.answer: Set appropriate expectations with stakeholders
questions.explanation: The summary says 'First, make sure to set appropriate expectations with stakeholders.' Optimization, monitoring and data collection come after.

questions.question: In what sense is the universal workflow a loop rather than a straight line?
questions.answer: The final deployment step (monitor and keep collecting data) feeds the next generation's data collection and development. Concept drift guarantees that each model will eventually need replacing.
questions.explanation: This combines the maintenance bullets and the last summary item with p.212.

questions.question: Without looking, can you name the three steps of the 'define the problem' phase?
questions.answer: Understand the broader context (end goal and constraints); collect and annotate a dataset and understand it in depth; choose how to measure success and which validation metrics to monitor.
questions.explanation: From the summary's first bullet.
